clue.text: Hanger-on demands Brazilian building land ?

parts.note: Para (Pará) is a Brazilian state and port, as in Para rubber and Para nuts
a site is a plot of land to build on

explanation.surface: A freeloader makes demands about a plot of Brazilian land for development.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brazilian' looks like an adjective for the land but is a word of its own: Para, the Brazilian state, gives PARA.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasite is someone who lives off others, a sponger who hangs on to a patron.

clue.text: Poet shows mounting skill, in a measure

indicators.note: in says the reversed word for skill goes inside the measure

parts.note: a perch is an old measure of length, five and a half yards

indicators.note: mounting, in a down clue, means the word for skill is read upwards

parts.note: art is skill, as in the art of conversation

explanation.surface: A poet displays growing ability in metre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounting' turns ART into TRA, which goes inside PERCH. 'measure' suggests poetic metre but is the old unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrarch was the fourteenth-century Italian poet famed for his sonnets to Laura.

clue.text: Artist uses odd term about Ibsen's work

indicators.note: about says the scrambled word goes around the name of the play
odd says the letters of term are to be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
Brand is an 1865 verse drama by Henrik Ibsen

explanation.surface: A painter adopts a strange expression when discussing a Norwegian play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' rearranges TERM into REMT, which goes 'about' BRAND, Ibsen's verse play.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt was the great seventeenth-century Dutch painter.

clue.text: Warner finds a captivating girl

explanation.surface: A man named Warner meets an enchanting young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warner' looks like a surname; it means something that warns.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm such as a police car's hooter warns; in myth the Sirens were alluring women who lured sailors.

clue.text: Put case for china manufacturers ?

indicators.note: manufacturers make things up, so the letters of the fodder are to be made into something new

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone argues the case for porcelain makers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put case for' reads as arguing a case; 'manufacturers' remakes PUTCASE, and 'china' means porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: Teacups are typical pieces of china, the porcelain crockery.

clue.text: Natives raised on farm ?

explanation.surface: Local people brought up in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natives' reads as people born in a place; it means people of Sweden, while the swede is a root vegetable a farmer grows.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Sweden are Swedes; a swede is also a turnip-like root crop grown on farms.

clue.text: Crossing the county ?

parts.note: read as a place where a stream may be waded through, and also as an Irish county

explanation.walkthrough: A water ford is a crossing; the whole name is also a county in the south-east of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterford is an Irish county; split, it describes a shallow crossing place in a river.

clue.text: Foreign woman finds same gir upsetting

parts.note: do. is the old abbreviation for ditto, meaning the same

indicators.note: upsetting, in a down clue, turns the girl's name upside down so it reads upwards

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A woman from abroad finds the same girl distressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'same' is DO, short for ditto; 'upsetting' turns ANN upwards to NNA.
explanation.definitionFit: Donna is Italian for woman or lady.

clue.text: Termagants give direction on minor ailments

indicators.note: on, in a down clue, puts the direction letter on top of the ailments

parts.note: S stands for south, a compass direction
colds are minor illnesses

explanation.surface: Bossy women give instructions on how to treat sniffles.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is a quarrelsome, nagging woman, a shrew who rails at people.

clue.text: Offer to carry fuel ?

explanation.surface: A bid is made to haul coal.
explanation.walkthrough: A tender is also the wagon behind a steam locomotive that carries its coal and water.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a bid is to tender; a locomotive's tender is the truck holding its coal.

clue.text: Duller passage written of an oriental conqueror

parts.note: tamer means less lively, so duller
a lane is a narrow way or passage

explanation.surface: A dull bit of prose was written about an eastern warlord.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamerlane (Timur) was the fourteenth-century Central Asian warlord who conquered much of western Asia.

clue.text: Some Puritan going to dance ?

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Is a strict Puritan really off to dance?
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a Latin American ballroom dance.

clue.text: Island is right in a group of them

indicators.note: in tells us the letter for right sits inside the name of the island group

parts.note: the Aran Islands are a group of islands off Galway, so 'a group of them' (islands) is ARAN

explanation.surface: This island is the correct one within an archipelago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'them' points back to 'Island': the Aran Islands, off the west coast of Ireland, hold the R. Arran itself is a Scottish island in the Firth of Clyde.
explanation.definitionFit: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde, off western Scotland.

clue.text: Foreign articles worker gets in a surreptitious way

parts.note: un is French for 'a', an indefinite article
der is German for 'the', a definite article
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A labourer acquires imported goods by stealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' reads as goods but means grammatical articles: French UN and German DER.
explanation.definitionFit: Done underhand means done secretly or deceitfully, slyly out of sight.

clue.text: The star is able to work

parts.note: can means is able
an opus is a work, especially a musical composition

explanation.surface: A celebrity performer is fit to go back on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The star' suggests a celebrity; it is a literal star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Canopus is the second-brightest star in the night sky, in the constellation Carina.

clue.text: Vessel joined by soldier with some hesitation

parts.note: a private is a soldier of the lowest rank
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A ship is boarded by a hesitant soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A privateer was an armed ship privately owned but licensed to attack enemy shipping.

clue.text: Island ways of speech

indicators.note: of speech says the word is to be taken as spoken, by its sound

parts.note: roads are ways for travelling

explanation.surface: An island's various manners of talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ways of speech' reads as dialects; 'ways' means roads and 'of speech' asks for the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodes is a large Greek island in the Dodecanese.

clue.text: Running away from work, in principle

indicators.note: in says the word for work goes inside the word for principle

parts.note: an element is a basic principle, as in the elements of geometry
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Fleeing from a job is, in theory, acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in principle' reads as 'in theory'; 'principle' is ELEMENT and 'in' puts OP inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Running off secretly to marry is to elope.

clue.text: Nurse got a sort of fish

indicators.note: a sort of hints that the letters are sorted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A nurse caught some kind of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a sort of' reads as 'some kind of'; 'sort' rearranges NURSEGOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The sturgeon is a large fish whose roe is caviar.

clue.text: That's the length, within a couple of feet

definitions.text: That's the length, within a couple of feet

parts.words: That's the length, within a couple of feet
parts.note: the clue describes a measure of distance spanned between your two feet as you walk, not a measurement in feet as units

explanation.walkthrough: 'a couple of feet' looks like two feet as a unit of measure (about 60cm); it means the walker's own two feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A pace taken in walking is measured from one foot to the other, the distance covered in one step.

clue.text: Side of an eastern loch

parts.note: Loch Leven is a loch in Scotland

explanation.surface: The shore of a Scottish lake to the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side' reads as a shore; it means a sports team. Loch Leven is a lake in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket or football team has eleven players, so a side is an eleven.

clue.text: Deciphered when drawn up ?

explanation.surface: Worked out when written up.
explanation.definitionFit: To decipher writing is to manage to read it; a cheque or document drawn up is written out for someone.

clue.text: Girl makes scholar take it up, poor lad

parts.note: MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate scholar

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, says it is written upwards
poor says the letters of lad are in poor shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl gets a learned man to take on a struggling boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns IT to TI; 'poor' rearranges LAD to LDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Matilda is a girl's name.

clue.text: Business intrigue, perhaps

explanation.surface: Is this commercial dealing a scandal?
explanation.definitionFit: An affair is a matter or concern, and also a secret love liaison.

clue.text: Business morning with ten breaks ? Heavens !

parts.note: a firm is a business company
a.m. stands for ante meridiem, morning

indicators.note: breaks says the letters of ten are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: An office morning interrupted by ten coffee breaks prompts a cry of dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' looks like rest breaks; it rearranges TEN into ENT. 'Heavens!' looks like an exclamation but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The firmament is the vault of the sky, the heavens above.

clue.text: Fleeces men in game ?

explanation.surface: Cheats the players in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'men in game' are chessmen: the rook is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To rook someone is to swindle them; rooks are also castle-shaped chess pieces.

clue.text: Bound over plain ?

explanation.surface: Placed on probation without any fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound over' looks like a legal phrase (put on a promise of good behaviour); it means leapt over, as a horse clears a fence.
explanation.definitionFit: To leap over a fence is to clear it; something plain is obvious and easy to see.

clue.text: Social class, in the Incas' terminology

indicators.note: in says the answer lies inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A rank in society, as named by the Incas.
explanation.walkthrough: The run spans the join of 'Incas'' and 'terminology'.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary social class, as in the Hindu system.

clue.text: Join a party — be a brick !

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A friend is urged to come along to the celebration and be a good sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be a brick' sounds like 'be a good sport'; here 'a brick' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Adobe is a sun-dried mud brick used in building in hot dry regions.

clue.text: They mother foreign types in Shropshire

parts.note: elles is French for 'they' (feminine)
mere (mère) is French for mother

explanation.surface: Women from abroad raise children in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foreign types' says both words are foreign, here French. Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border, and the answer is a market town there.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellesmere is a market town in north Shropshire, known for its meres or lakes.

clue.text: Rearrange the letters of Cromer, for example?

explanation.surface: A puzzle setter fiddles with a seaside place name.
explanation.walkthrough: Cromer is a seaside town on the Norfolk coast in England. 'Rearrange the letters' tempts an anagram of Cromer, but it is a definition: sort again.
explanation.definitionFit: To sort the letters again is to put them in a new order; Cromer is a coastal holiday town.

clue.text: Edward's favourite sage on TV. possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that these letters may be put in another order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A wise expert on television might be a king's favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: Piers Gaveston was the favourite of King Edward II of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Piers Gaveston was the notorious courtier and confidant of Edward II, executed in 1312.
